Tomato_Bacterial_Spot.symptoms: Small, brown, water-soaked, circular leaf spots with yellow halo; defoliation of older leaves; small water-soaked spots on green fruit that become irregular, light brown, sunken and scabby.
management: Use disease-free seed
Spray Streptocycline 40-100 ppm (20 g/acre)

Tomato_Early_Blight.symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings in a bullseye pattern, yellow margin; fruit infected through calyx/stem attachment with brown concentric rings.
management: Remove and destroy crop debris; crop rotation
Seed treatment: Trichoderma asperellum @ 4g/kg seed
Spray one of: Iprodione 50% WP @ 600 g/ac, Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 200 ml/ac, Mancozeb 35% SC @ 1 kg/ac, or several other listed fungicide options (see source for full list)

Tomato_Late_Blight.symptoms: Water-soaked black lesions on leaves/stems, rapidly expanding to necrosis; white sporulation on leaves; dark brown lesions and soft rot on fruit.
management: Ensure proper drainage; crop rotation
Soil application of Trichoderma asperellum (viride) @ 1.0 kg/acre
Spray one of: Cyazofamid 34.5% SC @ 80 ml/ac, Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 200 ml/ac, Mancozeb 35% SC @ 1000 g/ac (see source for full list)

Tomato_Septoria_Leaf_Spot.symptoms: Small round-to-irregular spots with grey centre and dark margin; spots coalesce causing blight and complete defoliation; stems and flowers also affected.
management: Remove and destroy affected plant parts
Seed treatment: Trichoderma asperellum @ 4g/kg seed
Spray Fluxapyroxad 250 g/l + Pyraclostrobin 250 g/l SC @ 200-250 ml/ha

Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.causal_organism: Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (TLCV), vectored by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci)
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Severe stunting; downward rolling/crinkling of leaves; older leaves leathery and brittle; shortened internodes; bushy appearance from excess lateral branching.
management: Raise nursery under protected conditions
Grow sorghum, maize, or bajra as a barrier crop
Use disease-free seedlings
Yellow sticky traps @ 5/acre
Remove alternate weed host (Abutilon indicum)

Spray one of: Dimethoate 30 EC @ 200 ml/ac, Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 200 g/ac, Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 200 ml/ac (targets the whitefly vector, not the virus itself — there is no direct antiviral treatment)
Note: this treatment targets the whitefly vector — the virus itself is not curable once a plant is infected; there is no direct antiviral treatment.

Tomato_Mosaic_Virus.causal_organism: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (labeled by TNAU as "Tomato Mosaic Virus" causal organism; some naming overlap in literature between ToMV and CMV, not fully disambiguated here)
Tomato_Mosaic_Virus.symptoms: Light/dark green mottling on leaves; wilting of young leaves; leaflet distortion and puckering; "fern leaf" and "shoestring" symptoms; stunted growth.
management: Use disease-free seeds
Remove infected plants
Crop rotation

Tomato_Spider_Mites.causal_organism: Red spider mite, Tetranychus spp. (a mite pest, not a fungal/bacterial disease)
Tomato_Spider_Mites.symptoms: Affected leaves turn reddish-brown and bronzy; severe infestation produces silken webbing on leaves, which wither and dry; flower and fruit formation affected.
management: Spray wettable sulphur 50 WP @ 2 g/litre, or dicofol 18.5 EC @ 2.5 ml/litre

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.causal_organism: Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva / Cladosporium fulvum)
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green/yellow spots without well-defined margins on upper leaf surface, turning distinctly yellow; olive-green velvety mold visible on the lower leaf surface; lesions coalesce in severe cases, foliage dies; primarily a disease of high-humidity greenhouse-grown tomatoes, less common in open field.
management: Improve ventilation/air circulation — stake and prune plants, space them further apart
Avoid wetting leaves when watering
Remove crop residue/debris from the field; rotate with non-tomato vegetables
Preventative fungicide program: chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper-based fungicide
Grow resistant cultivars where available
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.source: Not TNAU-sourced (no dedicated Indian-source coverage found) — consensus across Clemson HGIC (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/tomato-diseases-disorders/), UMass Amherst CAFE (https://ag.umass.edu/vegetable/fact-sheets/tomato-leaf-mold), University of Kentucky (https://veggiescout.mgcafe.uky.edu/node/154).

Tomato_Target_Spot.symptoms: Starts on older leaves, spreading upward; small necrotic lesions with light-brown centers and dark margins on leaves, sometimes with a ring/target pattern; on fruit, brown slightly sunken flecks that develop into larger pitted areas; spreads rapidly in wet weather and can defoliate/destroy the whole plant. Important disease in tropical/subtropical regions, relevant to Indian growing conditions.
management: Cultural: check seedlings in nursery before transplanting; avoid planting new crops next to old infected ones; remove lower leaves after fruit trusses are picked; weed control
Chemical: fungicides proven effective include chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, boscalid, and a famoxadone+mancozeb combination product
Resistance management: rotate fungicide classes — strobilurin-resistant strains of C. cassiicola have been documented, so repeated use of the same fungicide class risks resistance development
Tomato_Target_Spot.source: Not TNAU-sourced — University of Florida IFAS Extension (https://ipm.ifas.ufl.edu/pdfs/Target_Spot.pdf, https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/PP351).

management: No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.

Chili_Bacterial_Spot.symptoms: Small circular/irregular, dark brown to black greasy spots on leaves; spots enlarge with a lighter center surrounded by a dark band; spots coalesce into irregular lesions; severely affected leaves turn chlorotic and fall off; petioles and stems affected, stem infection causes cankerous growth and branch wilting; on fruit — round, raised, water-soaked spots with a pale yellow border that turn brown with a depressed center, sometimes showing bacterial ooze droplets.
management: Spray mancozeb @ 2 g/litre or copper oxychloride @ 2.5 g/litre
Seed treatment with 0.1% mercuric chloride solution for 2-5 minutes
Seedlings may be sprayed with 1% Bordeaux mixture or 0.25% copper oxychloride
Do not spray streptomycin after fruit formation begins
Field sanitation important; obtain seeds only from disease-free plants
No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.

Potato_Early_Blight.symptoms: Oval-to-angular dark brown/black "target" spots on leaflets with concentric rings of dead tissue, narrow chlorotic (yellowing) halo around each spot; lowest/oldest leaves infected first; can cause leaf droop and yield loss if severe; tuber lesions are less common than leaf infection but appear as sunken, dark, circular spots.
management: Cultural: crop rotation, remove and destroy infected debris, avoid overhead irrigation, keep plants adequately fertilized (stressed plants are more susceptible)

Chemical: Mancozeb applied as foliar spray @ 0.25% (with 1% urea) at 40-45 days crop age, repeated at 8-10 day intervals; for higher disease pressure, alternating with a systemic fungicide like hexaconazole 5 EC @ 0.05% between mancozeb sprays improved control further
Use resistant/late-maturing varieties where available
Potato_Early_Blight.source: Field trial conducted at Potato Research Station, S.D. Agricultural University, Deesa, India (2015-16 and 2016-17) — https://www.academia.edu/129963294 and https://www.academia.edu/116758209. (TNAU's own page exists but blocked automated fetching; this Indian field-study source was used as a substitute.)

Potato_Late_Blight.symptoms: Affects leaves, stems, and tubers. Water-soaked spots on leaves that enlarge, turning purple-brown then black; white fungal growth on the underside of leaves; spreads to petioles and stems, frequently developing at nodes, causing the stem to break and the plant to topple; tubers show purplish-brown spots that on cutting reveal rusty-brown necrosis spreading from the surface toward the center.
management: Protective spraying with mancozeb or zineb @ 0.2% to prevent tuber infection
Minimize tuber contamination by avoiding injury at harvest and not storing visibly infected tubers
Recommended resistant varieties (India-specific): Kufri Naveen, Kufri Jeevan, Kufri Alenkar, Kufri Khasi Garo, Kufri Moti
Destroy foliage a few days before harvest (via suitable herbicide) to reduce tuber contamination risk
Favourable conditions to watch for: relative humidity >90%, temperature 10-25°C, night temperature ~10°C, cloudiness before rainfall
No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.

Corn_Common_Rust.symptoms: Minute flecks appear on both leaf surfaces; circular-to-elongate cinnamon-brown, powdery, erumpent (bursting-through) pustules on both surfaces; pustules turn brownish-black as the crop matures; in severe cases, infection spreads to the leaf sheath and other plant parts. Alternate hosts: Oxalis europea, O. corniculata, O. stricta (common wood-sorrel weeds) — the pathogen needs these to complete its life cycle before infecting maize. Favourable conditions: cool, warm, moist weather (15-25°C).
management: Remove alternate host weeds (Oxalis species) near the field
Collect and destroy (burn or bury) crop remains after harvest
Foliar spray: kresoxim-methyl 44.3% SC @ 1 ml/litre, OR tebuconazole @ 1 ml/litre, OR chlorothalonil/mancozeb @ 2 ml/litre — applied at 35 and 50 days after sowing (DAS)

Corn_Northern_Leaf_Blight.causal_organism: Exserohilum turcicum (and Helminthosporium maydis, per TNAU's listing)
Corn_Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: (TNAU catalogs this as "Leaf Blight" — matches Northern Leaf Blight / Turcicum Leaf Blight, same disease.) Long, cigar-shaped, grey-green to tan lesions on lower leaves first; lesions are slender/oblong, tapering at the ends, 1-6 inches long; run parallel to leaf margins and coalesce to cover the entire leaf; spores produced on the underside of the leaf, giving a dusty black/green fuzz appearance below the lesions; affected leaves become greyish-green and brittle, resembling frost damage. Favourable conditions: wet, humid, cool weather, typically later in the growing season.
management: Burn or bury infected maize stubble after harvest
Foliar spray: mancozeb or zineb @ 2-4 g/litre, OR propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/litre — applied at 35 and 50 days after sowing (DAS)

Corn_Gray_Leaf_Spot.symptoms: Rectangular, narrow lesions bound by leaf veins, tan-to-gray in color, running parallel to the leaf veins; lesions can coalesce and cause significant blighting under heavy pressure; particularly damaging in warm (~27°C/80°F), high-humidity conditions (RH ≥90% for 12+ hours).
management: Cultural: crop rotation and residue/stubble management (the pathogen survives in maize residue between seasons, so reduced-till/no-till/continuous maize cropping increases risk); use genetically resistant hybrids where available — considered the most economical long-term control

Chemical: foliar fungicide applications with propiconazole or mancozeb have been shown to significantly reduce disease severity and improve yield in field trials — most effective when applied early, as disease severity reaches 2-3% of leaf area affected, and while lesions are still confined to the lowest 5 leaves
Corn_Gray_Leaf_Spot.source: Not TNAU-sourced (not among TNAU's 5 listed maize diseases) — PubMed/Plant Disease journal (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30870945/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18943592/), Pioneer Seeds agronomy guide (https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/gray_leaf_spot_cropfocus.html).

management: No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.

Rice_Brown_Spot.causal_organism: Helminthosporium oryzae (syn. Drechslera oryzae; sexual stage: Cochliobolus miyabeanus) — also called sesame leaf spot / Helminthosporiose / fungal blight
Rice_Brown_Spot.symptoms: Starts as minute brown dots, becoming cylindrical-to-oval-to-circular, resembling sesame seeds (0.5-2.0mm), coalescing into large patches that dry up the leaf; also infects panicle/neck (brown coloration) and seeds (black/brown spots on glumes, covered by an olive velvety growth); infected seed causes germination failure, seedling mortality, and reduced grain quality/weight; up to 50% yield loss in severe cases. Attacks from seedling (nursery) stage through to milk stage in the main field. Favourable conditions: 25-30°C, relative humidity above 80%, leaves wet 8-24 hours for infection; excess nitrogen aggravates it; notably common in nutrient-deficient or unflooded soils, rare in fertile, well-irrigated soils.
management: Cultural: use disease-free seed (disease is seed-borne); remove alternate/collateral weed hosts; grow resistant varieties — ADT 44, PY 4, CORH 1, CO 44, Cauvery, Bhavani, TPS 4, Dhanu; ensure proper nutrition and avoid water stress (most important preventive factor); amend silicon-deficient soils with calcium silicate slag and irrigate well

Seed treatment: Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10g/kg seed + seedling dip @ 2.5kg/ha in 100L water for 30 min; OR Captan/Thiram @ 2.0g/kg seed; OR hot water seed treatment (53-54°C for 10-12 min, after pre-soaking in cold water 8 hours)

Chemical: spray Mancozeb @ 2.0g/litre OR Edifenphos @ 1ml/litre, 2-3 times at 10-15 day intervals, preferably early morning or afternoon during flowering and post-flowering; tricyclazole seed treatment followed by mancozeb+tricyclazole spray at tillering and late booting stages also gives good control

Rice_Leaf_Blast.causal_organism: Magnaporthe oryzae (syn: Pyricularia grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
Rice_Leaf_Blast.symptoms: (TNAU treats Leaf Blast and Neck Blast as manifestations of one disease — "Blast" — at different plant sites; both classes share the same causal organism/source.) Attacks the crop from seedling to late tillering and ear-heading stages; appears on leaves, nodes, rachis, and glumes. Leaf blast: small bluish-green flecks that enlarge under moist conditions into spindle-shaped spots with a grey center and dark brown margin; spots coalesce, large leaf areas dry and wither; severely infected fields appear "burnt" from a distance. Nodal blast: black lesions girdle the nodes; affected nodes may break, killing all plant parts above the infected node. Neck blast: grayish-brown lesions on the neck, girdling it and causing the panicle to fall over; if infection occurs before the milky stage, no grain forms at all; later infection produces poor-quality grain. Favourable conditions: intermittent drizzles, cloudy weather, high relative humidity (93-99%), low night temperature (15-20°C, or below 26°C), presence of collateral/alternate host weeds, excess nitrogen application. Collateral (alternate) hosts: Panicum repens, Digitaria magrginata, Brachiaria mutica, Leersia hexandra, Echinochloa crusgalli.
management: Grow resistant/moderately resistant varieties: CO 47, CO 51, CO 52, CO 53, CO 55, CO 56, ASD 18, IR64
Remove and destroy weed hosts on field bunds and channels
Seed treatment: Captan, Thiram, Carbendazim, or Tricyclazole @ 2g/kg seed, OR Bacillus subtilis @ 10g/kg seed
Nursery spray: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 25g, or Edifenphos 50 EC @ 25ml, per 20-cent nursery

Main field foliar spray (at first symptoms): Edifenphos @ 200ml/acre, OR Carbendazim @ 100g/acre, OR Tricyclazole 75 WP @ 200g/acre, OR Iprobenphos (IBP) @ 200ml/acre, OR azoxystrobin + difenoconazole @ 100ml/acre
Rice_Leaf_Blast.source: TNAU Agritech Portal, in partnership with AICRIP (All India Coordinated Rice Improvement Project) and IRRI (International Rice Research Institute, Philippines) — https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/rice_diseases/rice_1.html and https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/rice_diseases/another%20methods_rice_1.html

Rice_Neck_Blast.causal_organism: Magnaporthe oryzae (syn: Pyricularia grisea, Magnaporthe grisea)
Rice_Neck_Blast.symptoms: (TNAU treats Leaf Blast and Neck Blast as manifestations of one disease — "Blast" — at different plant sites; both classes share the same causal organism/source.) Attacks the crop from seedling to late tillering and ear-heading stages; appears on leaves, nodes, rachis, and glumes. Leaf blast: small bluish-green flecks that enlarge under moist conditions into spindle-shaped spots with a grey center and dark brown margin; spots coalesce, large leaf areas dry and wither; severely infected fields appear "burnt" from a distance. Nodal blast: black lesions girdle the nodes; affected nodes may break, killing all plant parts above the infected node. Neck blast: grayish-brown lesions on the neck, girdling it and causing the panicle to fall over; if infection occurs before the milky stage, no grain forms at all; later infection produces poor-quality grain. Favourable conditions: intermittent drizzles, cloudy weather, high relative humidity (93-99%), low night temperature (15-20°C, or below 26°C), presence of collateral/alternate host weeds, excess nitrogen application. Collateral (alternate) hosts: Panicum repens, Digitaria magrginata, Brachiaria mutica, Leersia hexandra, Echinochloa crusgalli.
management: Grow resistant/moderately resistant varieties: CO 47, CO 51, CO 52, CO 53, CO 55, CO 56, ASD 18, IR64
Remove and destroy weed hosts on field bunds and channels
Seed treatment: Captan, Thiram, Carbendazim, or Tricyclazole @ 2g/kg seed, OR Bacillus subtilis @ 10g/kg seed
Nursery spray: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 25g, or Edifenphos 50 EC @ 25ml, per 20-cent nursery

Main field foliar spray (at first symptoms): Edifenphos @ 200ml/acre, OR Carbendazim @ 100g/acre, OR Tricyclazole 75 WP @ 200g/acre, OR Iprobenphos (IBP) @ 200ml/acre, OR azoxystrobin + difenoconazole @ 100ml/acre
Rice_Neck_Blast.source: TNAU Agritech Portal, in partnership with AICRIP (All India Coordinated Rice Improvement Project) and IRRI (International Rice Research Institute, Philippines) — https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/rice_diseases/rice_1.html and https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/rice_diseases/another%20methods_rice_1.html

management: No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.

Sugarcane_Red_Rot.symptoms: Reddening of the internal pith/stalk tissue (visible when the cane is split open), often with white patches interspersed in the red discoloration and a sour smell; on leaves — tiny reddish lesions on the upper leaf surface (2-3mm long, ~0.5mm wide), a minute red dot on the midrib that later becomes straw-colored in the center with darker fungal fruiting bodies (acervuli) developing; considered one of the most economically damaging sugarcane diseases in India ("the cancer of sugarcane"), causing severe losses in cane yield and sugar recovery in susceptible varieties; spreads rapidly in the rainy season, sometimes killing the entire crop.
management: Cultural: use disease-free planting material (setts); hot water treatment of setts before planting; crop rotation; field sanitation — remove and destroy infected plant debris; grow resistant/moderately-resistant varieties (variety resistance is not permanent, so periodic variety rotation is advised)

Biological: Trichoderma harzianum and Trichoderma viride strains (isolated from sugarcane rhizosphere soil) have shown strong biocontrol effect in Indian field trials — in one study, a T. harzianum strain fully controlled red rot in ~47-48% of treated canes and reduced severity substantially in the remainder, versus 97-100% infection in untreated canes; applied as a sett/soil treatment
Sugarcane_Red_Rot.source: TNAU Agritech Portal — https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/sugarcane_diseases/sugarcane_d4.html (page blocked automated fetching, content confirmed via indexed search snippets and secondary citations); supplemented with Indian Phytopathology / ICAR ePubs (https://epubs.icar.org.in/index.php/IPPJ/article/view/12862) and Sugar Tech journal (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12355-008-0028-7).

Sugarcane_Bacterial_Blight.symptoms: (Your dataset's "Bacterial Blight" class most likely corresponds to what is universally documented as Leaf Scald, the standard bacterial disease of sugarcane.) Hallmark symptom is a thin white "pencil line" (1-2mm wide) running from the midrib to the leaf margin, parallel to the veins, sometimes with a diffuse yellow border and reddish discoloration along part of its length; as the disease progresses, brown necrotic (dead) tissue develops from the leaf tip or margin, eventually covering the whole leaf, giving a scalded/burned appearance (hence the name); infection can be latent for years with no visible symptoms before suddenly causing wilting and death of mature stalks; spreads via infected cuttings/setts and contaminated cutting tools.
management: Important honest note: there is currently no effective chemical or biological treatment for leaf scald — multiple sources confirm control relies entirely on prevention.
Use resistant varieties (best available strategy)
Hot water treatment of seed cane before planting
Sterilize/disinfect cutting tools and implements between plants (prevents mechanical spread)
Avoid planting seedcane from any field with visible disease symptoms
Quarantine measures during germplasm/variety exchange between regions
Sugarcane_Bacterial_Blight.source: TNAU Agritech Portal (paddy expert system — despite the URL path, this page covers sugarcane leaf scald) — http://www.agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisleafscald.html; cross-confirmed by Texas A&M Plant Disease Handbook, USDA APHIS (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/sugarcane-disease), and a 2025 peer-reviewed review (https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/14/4/508).

management: No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.

Cotton_Bacterial_Blight.causal_organism: Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. malvacearum (also cited as X. campestris pv. malvacearum)
Cotton_Bacterial_Blight.symptoms: Attacks the plant at every stage from seed to harvest, with five recognized phases: (1) Seedling blight — small, water-soaked, circular/irregular lesions on cotyledons, spreading to the stem via the petiole, causing seedling withering and death; (2) Angular leaf spot — small dark-green water-soaked spots on the leaf underside, becoming angular (restricted by leaf veins) as they enlarge, turning reddish-brown with age, visible on both leaf surfaces; (3) Vein blight/vein necrosis (black vein) — veins and veinlets blacken, bacterial ooze forms as crusts on the leaf underside, affected leaves crinkle, twist inward, and wither, spreads to the petiole causing defoliation; (4) Black arm — dark brown-to-black lesions on stems/fruiting branches that can girdle them, causing premature leaf drop, stem cracking, gumming, and stems breaking to hang as dry black twigs; (5) Square rot/boll rot — water-soaked lesions on bolls turning dark/sunken, spreading through the whole boll, causing premature bursting, lint gets stained yellow by bacterial ooze and loses market value, seeds are also infected. Favourable conditions: soil temp ~28°C, air temp 30-40°C, relative humidity 85%, early sowing, delayed thinning, poor tillage, late irrigation, potassium-deficient soil; rain followed by bright sunshine in October-November is especially favorable.
management: Delint cotton seeds with concentrated sulphuric acid @ 100ml/kg seed
Treat delinted seeds with carboxin or oxycarboxin @ 2g/kg, OR soak seeds in 1000 ppm Streptomycin sulphate overnight
Remove and destroy infected plant debris; rogue out volunteer cotton plants and weed hosts
Crop rotation with non-host crops
Early thinning, early earthing-up with potash
Grow resistant varieties: Sujatha, 1412, CRH 71
Spray Streptomycin sulphate + Tetracycline mixture @ 100g, combined with Copper oxychloride @ 1.25 kg/ha
Cotton_Bacterial_Blight.source: eAGRI (Indian agricultural university e-course repository, Plant Pathology course PATH272) — http://eagri.org/eagri50/PATH272/lecture13/008.html

Cotton_Curl_Virus.causal_organism: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuV) — a begomovirus (family Geminiviridae), single-stranded circular DNA, bipartite genome
Cotton_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Downward and upward curling of leaves, thickening of veins, enations (small outgrowths) on the underside of leaves; in severe infection, all leaves curl and plant growth is retarded; boll-bearing capacity is reduced. One of the most economically damaging cotton diseases in India and Pakistan, with documented outbreaks causing 37-64% incidence in parts of northwest India (Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan) in some years. Vector/spread: transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci (viruliferous, i.e. virus-carrying whiteflies); alternate/cultivated host plants serve as year-round virus reservoirs; not transmitted by seed or contact — control must target the insect vector, not the plant directly.
management: Time planting dates to avoid peak whitefly vector population
Eliminate volunteer perennial cotton and alternate malvaceous hosts (e.g. wild okra)
Biological vector control: the fungus Paecilomyces farinosus parasitizes whitefly and reduces vector population
Foliar application of neem leaf extract + 1% neem oil — shown to reduce virus transmission by up to 80% in field studies
Granular systemic insecticides for direct vector management
Cotton_Curl_Virus.source: eAGRI Plant Pathology course — http://eagri.org/eagri50/PATH272/lecture13/009.html, cross-confirmed for Indian-context severity by peer-reviewed research (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7176085/, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7004920/)

Cotton_Fusarium_Wilt.symptoms: Yellowing and browning of cotyledons, followed by browning of the petiole; loss of leaf turgidity, yellowing, drooping, and wilting; browning/blackening of internal vascular tissue (visible as streaks when the stem is cut); infected plants are stunted with fewer bolls. Favourable conditions: soil temperature 20-30°C; hot, dry periods followed by rain; heavy black (alkaline) soils; excess nitrogen/phosphatic fertilizer; wounds from root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita) or Ash weevil grubs (Myllocerus pustulatus) increase susceptibility by creating entry points.
management: Remove and burn infected plant debris after deep summer ploughing
Apply farmyard manure or other organic manure @ 4 tonnes/acre
Mixed cropping with non-host plants to reduce soil temperature via shading
Treat acid-delinted seeds with Chlorothalonil @ 4g/kg seed
Seed treatment with Bacillus subtilis @ 10g/kg, OR Trichoderma asperellum @ 4g/kg
Soil application of Trichoderma asperellum @ 1kg/acre, twice — at sowing and again at 90 days after sowing (multiply 1kg of T. asperellum in 100kg farmyard manure for 15 days before application)
Spot drenching with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1g/litre water
No disease detected — this plant appears healthy. No treatment needed.
